Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA Ukraine Nato to ‘urgently’ get air defences for Ukraine, as Zelenskyy warns of surge in Russian missile production After Ukraine failed to shoot down a single ballistic missile fired by Russia on Wednesday, the president urged allies to increase supplies of Patriot interceptors Guardian staff and agencies Wed 5 Aug 2026 22.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 23.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday, and as Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Moscow was seeking to significantly boost missile ⁠production ahead of winter. Speaking at a National Security and Defense Council meeting on winter resilience, the Ukrainian president did not rule out the idea that stalling missile supplies from western allies were “aimed at making Ukraine , so to speak, more willing to compromise” in peace talks with Russia. Ukraine war briefing: Cut-price Patriot among options in desperate search for missile defence Read more After meeting Nato’s Mark Rutte, Zelenskyy said: “It is important to cut through all red tape and make the necessary political decisions. Literally every day, people’s lives here in Ukraine depend on the resolve of our partners in Europe and the United States.” Russia launched 24 ballistic missiles in an overnight attack on Wednesday , killing at least 17 people. Preliminary data from the Ukrainian air force showed its defences shot down 98 of the 115 drones fired by Russia overnight, but none of the ballistic missiles. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said that in the first half of 2026, supplies of air defence missiles from Ukraine’s allies had fallen to a third of their 2025 level. View image in fullscreen Ukrainian service members view a Patriot air defence system in 2024. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters The president also warned that Moscow was looking to significantly increase ballistic missile ⁠production as winter neared, when it is expected to renew its campaign against Ukraine’s energy sector. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on the development of defence technology, estimated that Russia was capable of launching 100 ballistic missiles every month to attack logistic ​hubs, industrial facilities, food stores and warehouses. “The war of attrition has entered its next phase,” he said on the Telegram app. Ukraine has been short on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles since the ⁠start of the war. But in recent weeks, an acute shortage has come into focus , with Moscow pummelling Kyiv, on ​average, every three days in July alone. Zelenskyy said the shortage of interceptor missiles was mainly caused by the war in the Middle East. Patriot missile systems are the only system in Ukrainian service able to intercept the Russian Iskander-M, S-400 and Zircon missiles, according to the Ukrainian air force. Russia often combines ballistic missiles with cruise missiles, drones and decoys, forcing defenders to track many threats and ration scarce interceptors, but Ukraine says it has too few batteries and interceptors to properly protect itself. View image in fullscreen Ukrainian firefighters work to put out a fire following a massive Russian ballistic missile and drone strike on Kyiv. Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images The interceptor shortage has become more acute as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has consumed large numbers of Patriot and other interceptors . An analysis by the Associated Press estimated that the US Patriot inventory had fallen by at least 65% since before the war. The Pentagon claims it retains a deep arsenal of supplies. Production cannot immediately close the gap. Lockheed Martin delivered more than 600 of the newest model of interceptors in 2025 and is working toward annual capacity of 2,000 by the end of 2030. But according to some estimates, Gulf states collectively fired more than 1,100 interceptors in the first three months of the Iran war. Nato says Europe’s first Patriot missile production facility is expected to open in September in Germany. Political signals from Washington have also shifted. At a Nato summit last month, Donald Trump said the US would give Ukraine a licence to produce Patriots . About three weeks later, he said he had not made a final decision . Even with a licence, officials and experts estimate that starting production in Ukraine would take years. Despite Trump casting doubt on the deal last month, the US is pressing ahead with talks on allowing Ukraine to make Patriot interceptors, according to reports from Reuters. The discussions ⁠include an option for Ukraine to ⁠build some components for final assembly elsewhere in ​Europe, according to the report. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.text: Image source, Inna Lytvynenko Image caption, Inna Lytvynenko says she was hunted by Russian drones when she tried to help a wounded woman in Kherson By Abdujalil Abdurasulov in Kyiv Published 6 hours ago Inna Lytvynenko always puts on her bright orange body armour when she's out on an emergency call. Last June, the paramedic was sent out in Kherson to treat a woman injured in a Russian drone attack, when an FPV drone smashed into her ambulance. Seconds later, she heard a buzzing sound in the sky. Another drone was flying straight towards her, fast. "I panicked. I grabbed my trauma bag and started running," she recalls. "I shouted and screamed. I knew that if I stopped, I would die." After chasing her for about 10 minutes, the drone flew away. Lytvynenko was quickly picked up by police. But what she called the "safari hunting" continued. Drones hit two more vehicles that arrived to take the injured woman to hospital. Hours later, a third police car finally managed to get her out. After another "safari" attack earlier this week, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called to put greater pressure on Russia in order to stop deliberate "hunting attacks" on civilians. Image source, Provided by a third party Image caption, The frequency of attacks on healthcare suggests that they are "a sustained feature of the war", MSF says Hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine are increasingly coming under Russian drone and missile attack, even though, according to the international rules of war known as the Geneva Conventions, they must be protected by all parties to the conflict. "This is a new normality, which should not be the normality," says Dr Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization's (WHO) representative in Ukraine. The WHO has registered 3,118 attacks on healthcare since the start of the Russian invasion in February 2022. "That's two cases per day," Habicht says. Since 2023 the number of attacks on healthcare has steadily grown. In 2024 it went up by 30%. Last year there was another 20% increase. This trend is expected to continue this year. A recent Doctors Without Borders (MSF) report , external says that Russia systematically and often deliberately targets Ukrainian medical facilities. The frequency of attacks on healthcare suggests that they are "a sustained feature of the war rather than an episodic consequence of large scale offensives," the report said. Last month Russian missiles hit a hospital in Kherson, badly damaging the building and killing one doctor. Hospital director Olena Tymoshenko believes it was a targeted attack. "It wasn't just one missile, there were three missiles that hit the hospital within a few minutes from each other. It cannot be an accident," she told the BBC. Figure caption, Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack Moscow also often uses a "double-tap" tactic, when they target the same location twice within a short period of time. Many believe that the second attack is deliberately aimed at first responders who arrive at the scene of the initial strike to rescue survivors. During a recent massive Russian air attack on Kyiv, seven people were killed, including a police officer and a volunteer, after a second strike on the same location. And lately Russian forces have been also targeting warehouses of humanitarian organisations. Last month alone, warehouses of three UN agencies, including the WHO, were damaged during air strikes. According to Habicht, the organisation shares coordinates of its facilities with both Moscow and Kyiv specifically in order to protect them from strikes. While missile and drone strikes can be indiscriminate, first-person view (FPV) drone strikes are almost always intentional. A drone pilot can see the target in a live feed from the drone's camera. So when it hits an ambulance, it has to be on purpose, says Robin Meldrum, MSF country coordinator in Ukraine. Dr Inna Lytvynenko says that she was wearing a uniform identifying her as a medical worker. The ambulance was also clearly marked. So, she believes the drone operator consciously chose to target them. Image source, Provided by a third party Image caption, A first drone hit Inna's ambulance in Kherson, while a second targeted her directly According to the WHO, strikes on ambulances make up 20% of all attacks on Ukraine's healthcare system, which suggests these are part of a calculated strategy. The result of such sustained attacks is that the civilian population close to the frontline are getting increasingly cut off from health services. The majority of people left in these areas are elderly people who often chronic diseases. Even if they survive air strikes and shelling, without medication and occasional check-ups they face a slow death. And ambulances may not be able to reach them if the risks are high. Lytvynenko and her colleagues constantly monitor social media to learn about threats. "It's really scary," she says. "Every time when we take a patient to hospital, we just pray. These drones can appear from anywhere, they can even get through anti-drone nets." In some cases, police are dispatched instead of ambulances. Since the danger zone where FPV drones operate is growing â as both Ukraine and Russia develop drones with greater and greater ranges â mobile clinics run by various health organisations have had to shift their operations further and further away from the frontline. "Two years ago, we could go up to 5-8km (3.1-5 miles) from the frontline," says Meldrum. "Now we won't go anywhere within 30km and this distance keeps growing." Over the past 18 months, MSF stopped regular visits to about 80 villages near the front where they had provided health services, says Meldrum. And recently it has paused ambulance services in Sloviansk, a major city in eastern Ukraine. "It doesn't feel like we're protected in this environment, and in the way that Russia is conducting the war," Meldrum says. "We don't feel that the rules of war are being respected." https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-p.text: WARSAW — European leaders are preparing to demand tougher sanctions on Russia at a summit on Thursday, putting them at odds with Donald Trump just days after the U.S. president struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports. The leaders plan to call for further sanctions and measures targeting Moscow's oil revenues at the European Council, according to a recent draft joint statement obtained by POLITICO, as EU governments reject Trump's claim to have secured an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. The disagreement exposes a widening divide over how to bring Moscow to the negotiating table. While Trump is seeking to bring down U.S. fuel prices by allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets, European leaders argue that restricting the Kremlin's energy revenues remains essential to forcing Putin to end the war. Advertisement Advertisement "Russia is not interested in deescalation, ceasing fire or peace," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a security conference in Warsaw on Monday. "That is why I will go to Brussels to ask my partners to consider seriously increasing sanctions against Russia." German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also called for further restrictions, pointing to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure despite Trump's announcement of a ceasefire. "Russia will only negotiate in good faith under pressure," Merz said Monday. "Following Moscow's reckless attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy supply, we must even tighten [sanctions] further." German Chancellor and leader of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) Friedrich Merz at the two-day retreat of the CDU leadership on Oct. 12, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images The push comes after EU foreign ministers on Monday approved the bloc's largest-ever addition to its Russia sanctions list, targeting more than 1,600 individuals and entities. The European Commission is also preparing a 23rd package of sectoral sanctions, which Kyiv expects to be circulated to EU governments by the end of the year, according to a senior Ukrainian official who was, like others in this article, granted anonymity to speak frankly on the sensitive negotiations. Other European countries are taking a similar position. Britain and Norway have also pledged to increase pressure on Moscow. "It's important to sanction Russia not to finance the war," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO, calling for loopholes in existing restrictions to be closed. Advertisement Advertisement Trump's election calculation Behind closed doors, many European diplomats see Trump's abrupt shift toward easing restrictions on Russian energy as driven primarily by domestic political concerns ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections. That is the "broadly held view" among EU officials, according to one senior official. The president is under mounting pressure over fuel prices, which have surged since the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Having promised during his 2024 campaign to bring gasoline prices below $2 a gallon, Trump now faces an electorate paying more than twice that amount, with Republicans at risk of losing control of Congress. His agreement with Putin is intended to release an additional 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel onto global markets over the coming months, easing pressure on fuel supplies and prices. But European and Ukrainian officials question whether the additional supply will make a meaningful difference, saying that the total volume promised amounts to only around 10 days of U.S. demand. They feel the deal risks undermining efforts to deprive Moscow of the revenues funding its invasion. "The reality" is that the additional fuel will have a "minimal" impact on U.S. prices, the senior EU official said. Advertisement Advertisement "This is about the midterms," a second EU official said. "He said he would bring down prices, but then he decided to go to war with Iran." The officials also question whether Putin intends to honor Trump's purported energy ceasefire. Russia has continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure since the announcement, while Kyiv says it was not consulted on the arrangement. For now, most European officials are reluctant to criticize Trump publicly, despite any doubts about the agreement. The EU and Ukraine should maintain their position over the coming weeks, when the administration's longer-term intentions toward Kyiv may become clearer, one diplomat said, adding that Trump might even change course again if Putin fails to deliver the promised diesel. Pressure on Washington The dispute has also revived European calls for Washington to enforce its own sanctions against Moscow. Tusk urged Europe and the United States to act together to show Russia they were prepared to impose tougher measures, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called on Washington to align its approach with Brussels. Kallas pointed to sweeping Russia sanctions legislation championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed into law last month but has yet to fully implement. Advertisement Advertisement The legislation gives Washington additional tools to target Russia's energy trade and those helping sustain its war effort. European officials want the administration to use them rather than loosen restrictions on Russian exports. Some Republicans are also calling for tougher action. "I think we need to be implementing the Russia sanctions bill," Republican Representative Dan Crenshaw told the Warsaw conference. The disagreement is raising wider questions in Europe about its dependence on Washington, particularly amid reports that U.S. officials have threatened to restrict Ukraine's access to American weapons unless Kyiv stops attacking Russian oil refineries. There is currently "no sign" Washington is following through on those threats, a NATO official told POLITICO, arguing that restricting sales would also hurt American weapons manufacturers. "PURL is a good deal for the Americans," the official said, referring to the NATO initiative under which European allies finance purchases of U.S. weapons for Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement European Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, without directly addressing the reports, said Europe needed to take "primary responsibility" for its own defense more urgently as Washington reduces its military presence on the Continent. The immediate test, however, comes on Thursday, when EU leaders will seek to maintain pressure on Moscow even as their most powerful ally moves in the opposite direction. Victor Jack and Sebastian Starcevic contributed reporting from Brussels, James Angelos contributed reporting from Berlin, Esther Webber contributed reporting from London.
